entries.title: 1 Chronicles 1:19
entries.description: A single verse tucked into a genealogy sits right on top of the Tower of Babel. A reflection on how names carried weight and how God leaves threads to pull on.
entries.body: "Eber had two sons. The first was named Peleg (which means 'division'), for during his lifetime the people of the world were divided into different language groups. His brother's name was Joktan." 1 Chronicles 1:19 (NLT) I do not usually highlight much in the genealogies. There are just a lot of names. A lot of so and so begat so and so. I read them, but I do not always stop. But this one made me stop. One man named his son Peleg, which means division. And during that son's lifetime, the people of the world were divided into different language groups. That is the Tower of Babel. This little verse, tucked into a long list of names, is sitting right on top of one of the most significant events in early Bible history. And it leaves me with so many questions. Did they name him knowing it was going to happen? Did God tell them ahead of time, the way He had spoken to others? Or was Peleg already born and growing up when the languages were divided, and they renamed him to mark the event? Or was it the other way around. Did they name him Peleg first, and then the division happened, and people looked back later and said, that name was prophetic ? It is kind of like the chicken or the egg. Today we just pick names because we like the sound of them. Back then, names meant something. Names carried weight. Names were tied to who you were, what was happening when you were born, or what God was doing in your family. A name was not just a label. It was a statement. So whoever named this child Peleg knew exactly what they were saying. I do not know which came first. But I love that even in the middle of a list of names, God left a thread for us to pull on. A little hint that there is more going on than just lineage. That every name on that list was tied to a real moment, a real family, a real story. It also makes me wonder how much of my own life is being marked by God in ways I do not see yet. The little details. The timing of things. The names of seasons I am walking through. What looks like a list of names to us was somebody's whole life. And every one of them mattered to God. Have you ever looked back and seen God's fingerprints on a season or a moment you did not pay much attention to at the time?

entries.title: 1 Chronicles 10:13
entries.description: Saul was the king God chose, yet he died unfaithful, consulting a medium instead of asking God. A reflection on running to Google, AI, and everyone else before God.
entries.body: "So Saul died because he was unfaithful to the Lord. He failed to obey the Lord's command, and he even consulted a medium instead of asking the Lord for guidance." 1 Chronicles 10:13 (NLT) The first king of Israel dies. And his sons die with him on the same day. The verse makes it sound like it did not have to end this way. Like maybe, if Saul had followed the Lord, he would not have died in that battle at all. But he did not follow Him. He failed to obey God's command. And on top of that, he went looking for guidance somewhere else. He consulted a medium instead of asking God. It is so easy to read this and get judgmental. Why would you do that? You are the king. You have access to God in a way most people did not at that time. Why would you go to a medium? But honestly. How often do we do the same thing in different clothes? We go to Google. We go to AI. We text three different friends to get their opinions. We poll people on social media. We ask anyone and everyone, and we never actually stop and ask God. It does not look like a medium to us. It looks normal. It looks responsible. We tell ourselves we are gathering wisdom or doing our research. But underneath it, the same thing is happening. We are running to every other source first, and God is not even in the conversation. And then we wonder why we feel scattered. Why we are anxious. Why we make a decision and immediately feel unsettled about it. The thing that gets me about Saul is that he was the one God chose. God picked him. Anointed him. Set him up to lead. And it ended like this, with the verse essentially saying he died because he was unfaithful. Being chosen did not protect him from his own choices. That is sobering. You can be called. You can be set apart. You can have every spiritual advantage. And you can still slowly drift, decision by decision, into a place where you are leaning on everything except God. Saul did not go from king to consulting a medium in a single day. That was the end of a long slide. Lots of small moments where he chose his own way. Lots of small moments where he did not ask. I want to be the kind of person who asks God first. Not last. Not after everyone else has weighed in. Not after I have already mostly made the decision and just want it confirmed. First. Where in your life have you been going to other sources before going to God?

entries.title: 1 Chronicles 14:10
entries.description: Two chapters after Saul dies for not seeking God, David asks God first, wins, gives Him the glory, and burns the idols. A reflection on cleaning house after the victory.
entries.body: "So David asked God, 'Should I go out to fight the Philistines? Will you hand them over to me?' The Lord replied, 'Yes, go ahead. I will hand them over to you.'" 1 Chronicles 14:10 (NLT) Just a couple chapters after Saul dies for not seeking God, we get David. The Philistines hear David has been anointed king, and they come out to find him. And what does David do? He asks God. Should I go out to fight them? Will you hand them over to me? It is such a contrast. Saul went to a medium. David went to God. And God answered him. Yes, go. I will hand them over to you. David goes. He wins. But the part that gets me is what he says when he comes back. He does not strut around taking credit. He does not say look what I did. He says God did it. He used me to burst through my enemies like a raging flood. He gave God the glory in the same breath as the victory. And the way it is written I can just hear his excitement behind God winning. I want to be like that. I want God to use me to burst through His enemies. I want to ask Him first, listen for the answer, move when He says move, and then come back and give Him the credit instead of acting like it was my own strength. But the verse keeps going. Right after that, it says David burned all the gods the Philistines had abandoned on the battlefield. He did not just win the battle. He destroyed the false gods. Winning was not enough. The fake gods had to go too. How often do we win a battle in our life, get past something hard, see God show up, and then leave the idols sitting right where they were? We celebrate the win, but we never deal with the things that pulled us away in the first place. David did not do that. He took the territory and then he cleaned house. What a difference from Saul. Saul lost his life because he would not deal with the things he should have dealt with. He kept what he was supposed to destroy. He went to sources he was not supposed to go to. David asked God, obeyed God, gave Him the credit, and burned the rest. Same nation. Same kind of pressure. Same enemies. Two completely different outcomes. Because one of them kept asking God. And one of them stopped. Is there a win in your life where you celebrated the victory but left the idols sitting on the field?

entries.title: 1 Chronicles 15:13
entries.description: David tried the Ark again, this time admitting they had failed to ask God how. A reflection on reverence, preparing your heart, and asking God how instead of rushing in.
entries.body: "Because you Levites did not carry the Ark the first time, the anger of the Lord our God burst out against us. We failed to ask God how to move it in the proper way." 1 Chronicles 15:13 (NLT) David finally gets it. The first time he tried to bring the Ark back, it ended badly. A man named Uzzah reached out to steady it and died on the spot. The whole thing got abandoned for a while. Now David is trying again. And before they move it, he stops and says this. We failed to ask God how to move it in the proper way. That line. They did not ask. They had good intentions. They wanted the Ark back. They were celebrating. But they moved it however they wanted instead of how God said to. And then David has the Levites consecrate themselves before they touch it. Purify themselves first. Treat it as sacred. Approach the things of God with the reverence God asked for. I read that and I wondered. Do we do that anymore? We just move. We just go. We do not stop and ask God how. We do not pause and ask if we are even supposed to. We do not prepare our hearts before we walk into something sacred. We just rush in and grab it and carry it however we feel like carrying it. And I started wondering why. Is it because Jesus came and broke the power of the law? He fulfilled it. We do not have to follow all the rituals anymore. There is not a literal Ark we are afraid to touch. Maybe. But I do not think the heart behind the law went away. The rituals pointed to something deeper. They pointed to a God who is holy. A God who is not casual. A God who wanted His people to prepare themselves before coming near to Him because He is worth the preparation. Jesus did not erase that. He made the way for us to come close. But coming close was never supposed to mean coming careless. I think we have gotten really comfortable with the things of God. And comfort is not the same as reverence. We can walk into worship while still mid-scroll. We can pray on the way out the door without ever stopping. We can grab a verse to post and never let it actually go down into us. Nothing happens. No one drops dead. But something is still missing. David's lesson was not just follow the rules. It was ask God how. Ask Him how to move forward. Ask Him how to handle the holy things. Prepare your heart before you walk in. That part still matters. What in your life are you carrying that you never stopped to ask God how to handle?

entries.title: 1 Chronicles 17:16
entries.description: David sits before God and asks who am I. A reflection on being fully known, failures and all, and still being chosen and used by God.
entries.body: "Then King David went in and sat before the Lord and prayed, 'Who am I, O Lord God, and what is my family, that you have brought me this far?'" 1 Chronicles 17:16 (NLT) I highlighted this one and then realized I had already written a highlighted blog about almost the exact same verse in 2 Samuel 7:18. They are nearly word for word. Accounting of the same story. Told twice. But I highlighted it again, when I got to it the second time. And I think there is a reason it stuck out to me again. David sits down in front of God after hearing this huge promise about his family and his line, and the first thing out of his mouth is not thank you. It is not I deserve this. It is a question. Who am I? What is my family? Why would you bring me this far? He goes on to say you speak as though I am someone great. You know what I am really like, and you still show me and my family favor. That is the part that stops me every time. You know what I am really like. He is not pretending. He is not standing in front of God acting humble. He knows himself. He knows his failures. He knows the parts of his story that should have disqualified him. And he is sitting in front of God in awe that none of it stopped God from using him. That is humbling in a way that goes deep. Because thousands of years later, sitting at my kitchen table reading this, I feel the same thing. Who am I that God would even want anything to do with me? He knows me. He knows what I am really like. He sees the things I have done and the things I have thought and the things I would not say out loud. And He still uses me. Still shows me favor. Still includes me in what He is doing. That is not small. I think that is why this verse keeps standing out in my reading. Because it is one of those truths I cannot soak in just once. The God of the universe chooses to use us. Not because we are great. Not because we have it together. But because that is who He is. And every once in a while, you just have to sit down in front of Him like David did and say it out loud. Who am I, that you would bring me this far? When was the last time you sat down in front of God and just let yourself be amazed that He chooses to use you at all?

entries.title: 1 Chronicles 20:5 & 7
entries.description: Two more giants fall in a single verse each, no fanfare. A reflection on how David
entries.body: "During another battle with the Philistines, Elhanan son of Jair killed Lahmi, the brother of Goliath of Gath. The handle of Lahmi's spear was as thick as a weaver's beam!" 1 Chronicles 20:5 (NLT) Then about another giant… "But when he taunted Israel, he was killed by Jonathan, the son of David's brother Shimea." 1 Chronicles 20:7 (NLT) I highlighted both of these and almost laughed at how casually they are written. Two giants. Two more relatives of Goliath. Both killed. Just one verse each. No big lead up. No taunting for forty days. No army standing around terrified. Someone just stepped up and took them down. And it made me think about Saul. Remember how long Goliath taunted Israel? Forty days. Forty days of a giant standing out there mocking God and mocking His people. And Saul, the king, the tallest man in Israel, the one who was supposed to lead, did nothing. The whole army did nothing. Until one boy showed up with a sling. David did not have armor that fit. He did not have experience. He did not have the title. He just had a deep belief that the God he served was bigger than the giant in front of him. And he killed him. Now, fast forward a few chapters in Chronicles, and giants are dropping like it is normal. Someone's brother. Someone's nephew. A guy named Elhanan. Jonathan, the son of David's brother. Just regular guys with regular names taking down giants and the writer barely makes a fuss about it. That is what one act of courage can do. David's courage did not just kill Goliath. It cracked something open in his generation. And the next one. And the one after that. People who used to be terrified watched a kid trust God and win. And something shifted. Giants stopped being unbeatable. They became something you just dealt with. Something you killed and moved on from. Not because the giants got smaller. But because the people got braver. Because they had a story to look back on. Because someone had gone first. I think about that a lot. How one person's faith can rewrite what the people around them believe is possible. How one act of obedience can echo for generations. David did not know that when he picked up those stones. He was just one boy trusting God on one day. But because he stepped out, his nephews and his soldiers and his soldiers' sons grew up in a different kind of Israel. A braver Israel. An Israel where giants get killed in a single verse with no fanfare. The future was changed because one boy decided to trust God. That is what courage does. It does not just win the battle in front of you. It changes what your kids and their kids believe God can do. Who are you going first for?

entries.title: Fall Into His Hands
entries.description: David sinned, faced consequences, and chose to fall into the hands of God rather than run. There is something different about mercy.
entries.body: "'I'm in a desperate situation!' David replied to Gad. 'But let me fall into the hands of the Lord, for his mercy is very great. Do not let me fall into human hands.'" 1 Chronicles 21:13 (NLT) David takes a census he was not supposed to take. And he gets punished for it. But God gives him a choice. Three options. And every single one is brutal. Three years of famine. Three months of being chased down and destroyed by his enemies. Or three days of plague. There is no good option. He is going to get a consequence. He just gets to pick which one. And David lands in a place I hope I would land too. He says I am in a desperate situation. But let me fall into the hands of the Lord, because His mercy is very great. Do not let me fall into human hands. He picked the option that put him in God's hands. Not because it would hurt less. Not because it was easier. But because he trusted who God is, even in the middle of consequence. Read that line again. His mercy is very great. That word stopped me. We talk all the time about how much God loves us. And He does. But David did not say let me fall into His hands because of His love. He said it because of His mercy. There is something different about mercy. Love is who God is toward us. Mercy is what we get when we have messed up and deserved otherwise. David had messed up. He knew it. He was not pleading innocent. He was not arguing the consequence was unfair. He had already confessed. He was just choosing where to land in the middle of it. And he chose the God whose mercy he already knew. I think if we really understood the mercy of God, it would change so much for us. Because we tend to run when we mess up. We hide. We avoid Him. We figure He must be done with us. We start trying to fix it ourselves before we come back to Him. But David ran toward Him. Even in discipline. Even in consequence. Even knowing it was going to cost him something. Because he knew. God's mercy is greater than what we deserve. His mercy holds us when we have earned the opposite. His mercy is the reason we can still come close, even after we have failed. I want to know God's mercy the way David did. Not just His love. His mercy. Because there will be seasons of consequence in my life. Seasons where I am facing the fallout of choices I should not have made. And in those seasons, the question is not going to be am I loved. The question is going to be where do I land? And I want to land in the hands of the One whose mercy is very great. When you have failed, where do you tend to run? Toward God or away from Him?

entries.title: It Has to Cost You Something
entries.description: David refused a free offering. He would not give God something that cost him nothing. That still convicts.
entries.body: "But King David replied to Araunah, 'No, I insist on buying it for the full price. I will not take what is yours and give it to the Lord. I will not present burnt offerings that have cost me nothing.'" 1 Chronicles 21:24 (NLT) This story is so cool, and it is so convicting if you actually sit with it. The Bible is supposed to convict, but so often we just want to skim through to feel good, not actually sitting with the hard. David is told to go up and build an altar to the Lord. He is told exactly where. So he heads up to this threshing floor that belongs to a man named Araunah. Araunah sees David coming and bows down. David tells him I need to buy this place from you. I have to build an altar here so this plague will stop. And Araunah says just take it. It is yours. Take the threshing floor. Take the oxen for the sacrifice. Take the wood. I will give all of it to you. I love picturing this moment. Maybe Araunah was begging him a little. Please. If this will stop the plague, take it. I will give it to you. Maybe he was scared. Maybe he was generous. Maybe both. And David says no. I will not take what is yours and give it to the Lord. I will not present burnt offerings that have cost me nothing. He insisted on paying full price. He was the king. He could have taken it. The man was already offering it. And David said no. Because something in him knew that an offering that did not cost him anything was not really an offering at all. I think about this so often when I walk into church. How easy it is to want to worship in a way that costs me nothing. How easy it is to live out a faith that does not actually require anything of me. I will sing the songs but not surrender the thing God has been asking me to surrender. I will say I love God on Sunday but not speak His name out loud at work on Monday. I will not even pray over a meal at a restaurant. Maybe that is where you are too. We try so hard to live a faith that costs us nothing. And I think that is exactly what Jesus was talking about when He said the road is narrow. The narrow road costs you something. Your comfort. Your image. Your time. Your money. Your reputation. Your plans. Something. If your faith has never cost you anything, it might be worth asking why. David understood it. He looked at a free altar, a free sacrifice, a free piece of land, and he said no. Not because it was a bad deal. Because his God deserved more than something free. The God who had shown him mercy was not going to get a leftover offering. That convicts me. Because I want my worship to cost me something. I want my faith to look like something other people can see is real. I want to be a person who does not just sing about surrender, but actually lays things down. Not because God needs my sacrifice. But because love that costs nothing is not really love. What are you offering God right now that has not cost you anything?

entries.title: A Man of Unusual Wisdom
entries.description: One small line tucked into a long list of names. A man of unusual wisdom. What line would be written next to yours?
entries.body: "The responsibility for the East Gate went to Shelemiah and his group. The North Gate was assigned to his son Zechariah, a man of unusual wisdom." 1 Chronicles 26:14 (NLT) I think I highlighted this just because in the middle of a lot of names and assignments and positions at the gates, this one guy had something a little extra next to his name, and it made me wonder why. The East Gate went to Shelemiah and his group. The North Gate was assigned to his son Zechariah, a man of unusual wisdom. That little line. A man of unusual wisdom. That was it. The whole description. No story to back it up. No sermon he preached. No big moment they tied it to. Just this one phrase tucked into a long list of names. But somebody knew. Somebody saw enough of his life to add that line. It makes me wonder how he got it. What did he do day in and day out that earned him that description? How did he show wisdom? Was it the way he handled conflict? The way he made decisions? The way he listened before he spoke? The way he treated people? The way he sought God? We do not know. The Bible does not tell us. But somebody who watched him over time decided that line needed to be in there. A man of unusual wisdom. And I just sat with that for a minute. Because if someone were writing about me, would they stop and add a line? Would there be one phrase that just naturally fit beside my name? And if so, what would it be? That is a hard one to think about honestly. We do not usually think about how we are being remembered while we are still living. We think about today. About the things on our list. About what we have to get through. But our lives are being summed up by the people around us in real time. Our coworkers. Our family. Our friends. Our kids. They are all watching, and they are slowly forming the line they would write next to our name. Zechariah did not earn his line in a day. He earned it over a life. The same way we do. The little choices we make. The way we respond when no one is looking. How we handle the small things. The quiet faithfulness no one is clapping for. It all adds up to whatever line ends up next to our name when it is all said and done. I do not want my line to be empty. I want there to be something. Even one phrase. One thing that was so consistent in my life that someone could not help but write it down. Something like she loved God. Or she was faithful. Or she was steady. Or she made room for people. Or she did not give up. Something true. If someone were writing about you, would they stop and add a line? And if so, what would it be? Drop it in the comments. I would love to read them.

entries.title: Be Strong and Do the Work
entries.description: David handed his son the plans, the vision, and the God he had walked with. Then he told him to be strong and not be afraid.
entries.body: "Then David continued, 'Be strong and courageous, and do the work. Don't be afraid or discouraged, for the Lord God, my God, is with you. He will not fail you or forsake you. He will see to it that all the work related to the Temple of the Lord is finished correctly.'" 1 Chronicles 28:20 (NLT) David has just been told he will not be the one to build the temple. His son Solomon will. It is easy to read that and think okay, that responsibility just shifted to Solomon now. But that is not really what happened. David did almost everything but the actual building. He had the plans. He organized it. He designated the gold for every dish. The silver for every utensil. The meat hooks. The incense. He had a plan for the chariot and the gold cherubim. The Bible says every detail of the plan was given to him by God in writing. He just was not the one who got to build it. So he passes all of it on to his son. The plans. The materials. The vision. The instructions God had given him personally. And then he says these words. Be strong and courageous, and do the work. I love that he does not just leave it at the positive. He flips it and says the same thing from the other side. Don't be afraid or discouraged. Both. Be strong. Do not be afraid. Be courageous. Do not be discouraged. He is covering it from every angle. Like he knows his son is about to step into something heavy and he wants to make sure nothing slips through the cracks. And then he tells him the reason. Because the Lord God, my God, is with you. He will not fail you or forsake you. My God. He is not just preaching at his son. He is testifying. This is what I know about the God I have walked with. He will be with you the same way He has been with me. There is something about that I keep turning over. David is handing his son the work, the plans, the vision, and the God he has known personally. He is not just giving him a project. He is passing on a relationship. Then there is one more line that I cannot get past. He will see to it that all the work related to the temple is finished correctly. He says God will see it through. Not Solomon. God. Which is interesting because we usually credit Solomon with building the temple. But the way David says it, the credit belongs to the Lord. Solomon would do the work. God would be the one to finish it correctly. That is a good reminder for me. The things God has called me to are not really mine. He gives the vision. He gives the resources. He gives the strength. He gives the people who help. And when it is all said and done, He is the one who sees it through to completion. I just have to be strong and courageous and do the work. I just have to not be afraid and not be discouraged. He handles the rest. What is something God has called you to that you have been carrying like it is all on you to finish?

entries.title: 1 Kings 13:23
entries.description: After the man of God had finished eating and drinking, the prophet who had brought him back saddled his donkey for him. A chapter about listening to God over man.
entries.body: "After the man of God had finished eating and drinking, the prophet who had brought him back saddled his donkey for him." 1 Kings 13:23 (NLT) This is just one verse from a whole disturbing chapter. If you have not read 1 Kings 13, stop and go read it before you keep reading this. It is short. It will not take long. And it is one of those chapters that will sit with you for a while. Here is the short version. A young prophet is sent by God with a clear word and clear instructions. Do not eat. Do not drink. Do not even go home the same way you came. On his way back, an older prophet meets him and invites him over. The young prophet says no at first. He remembers what God told him. But then the older prophet lies and tells him an angel said it was fine to come eat. So he goes. And later in the chapter, God takes his life because of it. I know how that sounds. It feels harsh. It feels like it does not fit. But this chapter really resonated with me a few years ago, and it has stayed with me ever since. Because how many times have we done the very same thing? God tells us something. We know what He said. We have read it. We have prayed about it. We have felt the conviction in our gut. And then someone comes along who sounds more spiritual. More religious. More seasoned. Someone with a bigger platform or a louder voice or more years in the church. And they tell us something different. And we listen to them over Him. That is the part that stopped me. We would rather listen to a man than to God. This is exactly why being in the Word matters so much. Not a book about the Word. Not a podcast about the Word. The actual Word. And it is why a real relationship with God, the kind where you know His voice for yourself, is not optional. It is the only thing that will keep you steady when someone who looks the part tells you it is okay to do the very thing God already told you not to do. There is one more piece of this chapter that I think matters. The older prophet, the one who lied, was not the one who paid for it. The young prophet was. The person leading you astray may walk away just fine. You are the one who has to live with the consequences of who you chose to listen to. Stay in the Word. Know His voice. Do not hand your faith over to anyone, no matter how spiritual they look. Where in your own life have you been tempted to trust a person over what God has already said to you?

entries.title: 1 Kings 17:9 & 12
entries.description: A starving widow heard from God before Elijah ever arrived. She had to start cooking with nothing, and provision showed up in the middle of obeying.
entries.body: "Go and live in the village of Zarephath, near the city of Sidon. I have instructed a widow there to feed you." "But she said, 'I swear by the Lord your God that I don't have a single piece of bread in the house. And I have only a handful of flour left in the jar and a little cooking oil in the bottom of the jug. I was just gathering a few sticks to cook this last meal, and then my son and I will die.'" 1 Kings 17:9 & 12 (NLT) I have read this story so many times. It is hard to even picture being in her place. Down to your last handful of flour. Gathering sticks to cook one final meal for you and your child. Planning to lay down and die after. But this time through, something hit me that I had never noticed before. Verse 9. God did not just send Elijah to her. He told Elijah, I have already instructed a widow there to feed you. He told her first. For years I read this and thought, seriously Elijah? You are going to walk up to a starving widow and ask her for the last of her food? But that is not what happened. God told him to go. And God had already spoken to her about it before he ever showed up. I cannot stop thinking about her side of that conversation. Imagine going about your day, completely hopeless, knowing this is the end. And in the middle of that, you hear from God. He says someone is coming. Feed him. If I am being honest, I think I would have questioned the whole thing. I would have thought I was losing it. God, I literally have no food. And You are telling me a stranger is about to show up wanting to eat? Then Elijah finally arrives, and the first thing he asks for is a cup of water. I wonder if he stopped there on purpose. Like he could see her. Could see the situation. Maybe he thought, I will just ask for water. Food is too much to ask of her. And I wonder if she felt a little wave of relief. Oh good. Water. I can do water. Please do not ask for food. But then he asks. And her answer tells you everything. I swear by your God, I have nothing but a handful of flour and a little oil. I am about to cook this last meal and then we are going to die. She knew. She had heard from God. But sitting there with empty hands, it still felt impossible. I think what gets me most is wondering if knowing made it easier. Did she have a little less fear because God had told her ahead of time? Did she have a thread of hope, even a small one, that maybe if she just obeyed, something would happen? Because Elijah does not wait until after she cooks to reassure her. He tells her right then, before she gives him a single bite, that if she does this, she will be provided for until the famine ends. That is the part I keep coming back to. God spoke to her in her hopelessness. He told her ahead of time. He sent provision wrapped up in what looked like another request. And the promise came before the obedience was finished. She had to start cooking with nothing. That is so much of what walking with God looks like. He tells us something. It does not match what we can see. We have to move before the math works out. And the provision shows up in the middle of the obeying, not before. Where is God asking you to start cooking with what feels like nothing?

entries.title: 1 Kings 18:46
entries.description: God just rained fire from heaven, but the verse Heather marked is Elijah outrunning a chariot. A reflection on the quiet kind of special strength God gives.
entries.body: "Then the Lord gave special strength to Elijah. He tucked his cloak into his belt and ran ahead of Ahab's chariot all the way to the entrance of Jezreel." 1 Kings 18:46 (NLT) It is kind of funny that this is the verse I highlighted. Because in the same chapter, God just rained down fire from heaven. He burned up a soaking wet altar in front of hundreds of people who had been worshiping a false god. That is the headline moment. That is the unforgettable scene. And yet this little verse at the end is what I marked. Elijah, with special strength from God, tucking his cloak into his belt and outrunning a chariot all the way to Jezreel. It almost sounds like a superhero story when you read it that way. And honestly that is part of why it stuck with me. It seems so unrealistic compared to everything else. But then I had to laugh at myself, because what God did with the fire was so much more impressive than a man running fast. I think the reason it stayed with me is what it says underneath the story. God gives special strength. Not just to prophets. Not just in dramatic moments. He gives it to His people, still, today. But here is the thing. Most of the time, that strength does not look like running ahead of a chariot. It looks like getting out of bed when you have not slept. It looks like showing up for your people when you have nothing left. It looks like finishing the thing you swore you could not finish. It looks like staying soft when life has handed you every reason to go hard. It looks like persevering when by every reasonable measure, you should already be done. That is special strength too. It is just quieter. No one is going to write a Bible story about the day you kept going when you wanted to quit. But God sees it. And He is the One giving you what you need to do it. Elijah ran. You might just be standing. Both take strength that does not come from you. Where do you need God to give you special strength right now?

entries.title: 1 Kings 22:5
entries.description: King Jehoshaphat paused to ask what the Lord said, then they heard the truth and did what they wanted anyway. A reflection on surrounding yourself with people who tell the truth, not yes men.
entries.body: "Then Jehoshaphat added, 'But first let's find out what the Lord says.'" 1 Kings 22:5 (NLT) I love this about King Jehoshaphat. He was not a negative guy. He was positive. He was on board. But before he committed, he stopped and said, let us find out what the Lord says first. That alone is something to sit with. But then it gets interesting. They called in 400 prophets. Four hundred. And all 400 said the same thing. Go, you will win. Here is what I never caught before. The text does not call them prophets of the Lord. They were just prophets. There is a distinction there, and it matters. Prophets were supposed to speak from God. So who were these 400? Why were they trusted? Were they just the yes men we so often find ourselves surrounded by? I think about how many churches are running exactly like this. The head pastor surrounded not by people who will seek God with him, but by people who will default to whatever he says and tell him yes. And honestly, in our personal lives, this is what we want too. We do not like to be corrected. We do not like to be challenged. A lot of us do not even have anyone in our life we trust enough to do that. So we end up with our own little circle of 400, all telling us what we already decided we wanted to hear. Then Jehoshaphat, again, pauses. He asks if there is a real prophet of the Lord they can ask. And the king of Israel basically says yes, there is one, but I hate him because he never says anything good about me. That line alone could preach. So they send for Micaiah. And when he walks in, he sarcastically tells them exactly what they want to hear. Oh yes, go, you will win. He knew the script. He knew what they were waiting on him to say. And they pushed back. Tell us the truth. So he did. And they got angry. And they did what they wanted to do anyway. That is the part that stings. They asked. They heard. They did not like it. So they moved forward like they never heard it at all. How often do we do that? We pray about something. We get an answer we did not want. So we keep asking, hoping someone else will tell us what we already decided. And when the truth finally comes, we get offended at the messenger and move forward anyway. There is so much in this chapter. Surround yourself with people who will seek God with you, not people who will just nod at you. Be willing to hear the truth even when it is not what you wanted. And when God speaks, do not ask just to ask. Ask to listen. Who in your life is willing to tell you the truth, even when it is not what you want to hear?

entries.title: Highlighted 1 Samuel 14:8
entries.description:
“All right then,” Jonathan told his armor bearer. “We will cross over and let them see us.”
1 Samuel 14:8 (NLT) I think I highlighted th...
entries.body: “All right then,” Jonathan told his armor bearer. “We will cross over and let them see us.” 1 Samuel 14:8 (NLT) I think I highlighted this verse because I had forgotten the story. That’s it. No big explanation. No immediate takeaway. I had forgotten how this moment unfolds. How Jonathan, without an army or approval, decides to move. He doesn’t wait for perfect conditions or a clear outcome. He doesn’t ask for permission or even ask his dad. He just moves. Reading it again felt like remembering something I once knew but had forgotten. I actually couldn’t wait to see how the story unfolded. It had some twists I didn’t see coming… the honey part especially. This verse reminded me that sometimes highlighting while reading the Bible is not always about insight. Sometimes it is about remembering. Remembering a story. Remembering a picture of faith that slipped out of my mind. I feel like I know the Bible. I’ve heard the stories. I’ve even taught them in children’s ministry. So coming across one that I wasn’t really familiar with anymore was interesting. I read about Jonathan’s courage, and it didn’t come from certainty. It came from trust. His plan wasn’t loud or strategic. It was simple. We will cross over… and let God determine what happens next. That line carries the weight of action. Faith that moves without guarantees. Faith that doesn’t need a crowd. I think I wanted to remember that. Not every highlighted verse has to explain something. Some just remind us of who God has been and how He has worked before. And maybe that is enough. Have you ever reread a passage and realized you had forgotten the story altogether? What made it stand out to you this time?

entries.title: Highlighted 1 Samuel 15:17
entries.description: “And Samuel told him, ‘Although you may think little of yourself, are you not the leader of the tribes of Israel? The Lord has anointed you king of...
entries.body: “And Samuel told him, ‘Although you may think little of yourself, are you not the leader of the tribes of Israel? The Lord has anointed you king of Israel.’” 1 Samuel 15:17 (NLT) This verse has stood out to me in the past. Not really understanding it in the middle of the story that was happening. And I have spoken on this story before, and it didn’t really make sense then either. What does it mean that Saul thought little of himself? He was the king. He had authority, position, and people following him. This was not someone hiding on the sidelines. So that description does not fit the way we usually think about insecurity. But Samuel spoke confidently. He was not just making a random statement. He was not reading Saul’s mind. He was watching Saul lead. Saul had just disobeyed God’s clear command. And when confronted, he did not own it. He justified his actions. He explained them. He blamed the people. The people wanted it. The people kept the best. The people pressured me. That is how Samuel knew. Thinking little of himself did not show up as humility. It showed up as an inability to stand firm when obedience would cost him approval. Samuel had walked with Saul long enough to recognize the pattern. He saw how Saul adjusted God’s commands to avoid conflict. How he shifted responsibility instead of repenting. How fear of people kept shaping his decisions. So Samuel brings it back to identity. You are the leader. God anointed you. In other words, you knew better. Saul wore the crown, but he did not fully carry the weight of leadership. His insecurity did not make him cautious. It made him flexible in the wrong places. That stopped me. Because it suggests that insecurity and people pleasing often work together. Thinking little of ourselves does not always protect us from disobedience. Sometimes it becomes the excuse for it. Samuel could see what Saul may not have wanted to admit. That his self perception was shaping his obedience. That his fear was louder than his faith. This verse makes me wonder how often our actions reveal what we believe about ourselves before we would ever say it out loud. And how often people who walk closely with God can see right through us, usually before we do. I am still sitting with this one. Because it makes me ask where do I shift responsibility when obedience feels costly. Where fear of people quietly overrides fear of God. What do you think Samuel saw in Saul? And how do you think insecurity shows up in leadership today?

entries.title: Highlighted 1 Samuel 16:18
entries.description: “One of the servants said to Saul, ‘One of Jesse’s sons from Bethlehem is a talented harp player. Not only that, he is a brave warrior, a man of wa...
entries.body: “One of the servants said to Saul, ‘One of Jesse’s sons from Bethlehem is a talented harp player. Not only that, he is a brave warrior, a man of war, and has good judgment. He is also a fine looking young man, and the Lord is with him.’” 1 Samuel 16:18 (NLT) When I went to this highlight, I had to go back and reread what comes before it. At this point, David has not fought Goliath. He has not led an army. He has not stepped into anything public that would earn a reputation like this. So how is he already being described as a brave warrior and a man of war? Scripture does not record David serving in the army yet. There is no battlefield moment. No public victory. And yet someone is describing him as if his courage and character are already known. That made me stop. Because maybe this is not about public battles. Maybe it is about how David lived where he was. Protecting sheep. Facing danger when no one else was around. Taking responsibility seriously even when no one was watching. David did not become brave when he stepped onto a battlefield. He brought his bravery with him. And that part stood out to me too. Who said this? Not Samuel. Not God directly. A servant. Someone who had simply been paying attention. David’s life was already speaking before his story became known. That made me think about how often faithfulness is formed quietly, long before it is ever seen publicly. How obedience in small, unseen places is actually preparation for something bigger. David had not fought the battle yet. But he was already becoming the kind of man who would. And someone noticed. What is being formed in your life right now that no one else sees yet?

entries.title: Highlighted 1 Samuel 22:1–2
entries.description: “So David left Gath and escaped to the cave of Adullam. Soon his brothers and all his other relatives joined him there. Then others began coming to...
entries.body: “So David left Gath and escaped to the cave of Adullam. Soon his brothers and all his other relatives joined him there. Then others began coming to him—men who were in trouble or in debt or who were just discontented. Until David was the captain of about four hundred men.” 1 Samuel 22:1–2 (NLT) I keep thinking about who chose to follow David. Not when he was officially on a throne. Not when everything looked established and impressive. But when he was hiding in a cave. That stood out to me. His brothers came first. The same ones who had mocked him when he showed up at the battlefield to fight Goliath. Then others came. The ones in trouble. In debt. Discontented. The misfits. David was not offering safety, comfort, or status. He was offering presence. He was in the middle of it himself. And that might be why they followed him. When people are already on the margins, they are not usually looking for someone polished with all the answers. They are looking for someone who understands the fight because they are in it too. David did not lead from a distance. He led from the same cave. That made me think about the Church. So often we assume people are drawn to excellence, polish, and perfection. And while those things can matter, people who are hurting are often drawn to something else. They want authenticity. They want honesty. They want someone who is not pretending they have it all together. People who are struggling do not need someone who looks untouchable. They need someone who has been touched by the same struggle and still trusts God. David’s leadership was formed in shared hardship, not in presentation. And God used that. It also made me stop and think about myself. It is always easier to look at others and see how the Bible applies to them. But this made me ask what kind of leader I am becoming. Am I willing to stay close to the mess? Do I value being present in the battle more than being seen as put together? David did not build an army by impressing people. He built it by walking with them through uncertainty. And God did something powerful with that. Do you think people today are drawn more to polish or presence?

entries.title: Highlighted 1 Samuel 30:24
entries.description: “Who will listen to you when you talk like this?” David demanded. “We share and share alike—those who go to battle and those who guard the equipmen...
entries.body: “Who will listen to you when you talk like this?” David demanded. “We share and share alike—those who go to battle and those who guard the equipment.” 1 Samuel 30:24 (NLT) What I love about this moment is how clear David is. Everyone matters. From the front lines to the supporting roles. David does not measure value by visibility. The ones fighting were not more important than the ones guarding the supplies. Different roles, same value. And he was firm about it. He does not present this as kindness. He presents it as leadership. This was not a suggestion. That stood out to me. Because it shows that biblical leadership is not situational. It is principled. David was not reacting emotionally. He was leading from conviction. And that conviction still applies. Strong leaders understand that teams need different roles to function. That success is shared. That unseen work is still essential work. That unity is protected when every role is valued. David leads the way God leads. He values people, not just outcomes. He protects dignity, not just productivity. He understands that the mission requires both action and support. That kind of leadership lasts. In families, in churches, in organizations, the leaders who build something meaningful are the ones who understand this. Value does not come from position. It comes from purpose. From the front lines to the background, everyone belongs. What are your thoughts on what David is saying here?

entries.title: Firmly Established and Drifting
entries.description: Rehoboam followed God when he was desperate. He abandoned Him when he was strong. We do the same thing.
entries.body: "But when Rehoboam was firmly established and strong, he abandoned the Law of the Lord, and all Israel followed him in this sin." 2 Chronicles 12:1 (NLT) This is a warning. Rehoboam had been following the Lord. He had been obeying. He had been blessed because of the choices he was making. And then the verse says it. When he was firmly established and strong, he abandoned the Law of the Lord. When things were finally good. When he was finally stable. When he finally had what he had been working toward. That is when he walked away. That is so sad. And it is so real. Because we do the same thing. We cry out to God when we are desperate. We follow Him close when we have nothing. We pray hard when we are broke and scared and unsure of how it is all going to work out. And then He blesses us. He provides. He answers. We get the house. We get the job. We get the family. We get the stability. And somewhere along the way, we forget who got us there. We get firmly established. And we drift. It does not usually happen all at once. It is slow. It is quiet. It is little choices that add up. We stop praying as often because we do not feel like we need to. We stop opening the Word because life is busy and good. We start trusting the systems we built instead of the God who built them. And then one day we look up and realize we are not even sure when He stopped being the center of our life. That is what happened to Rehoboam. But the part that wrecks me even more is the next line. And all Israel followed him in this sin. He did not fall alone. He brought a whole nation with him. That is exactly what we see today. Famous preachers fall, and people get pulled into defending the fall instead of grieving it. Famous artists come out with sin, and the church takes sides. People line up behind the person they loved instead of behind the truth. Established, strong, influential people abandoning the way of the Lord. And so many people following them in it. It is not a new story. It is the same one over and over. Which is why I keep coming back to this prayer. God, please help me to be firmly established and strong in You. Not in anything else. Not in my income. Not in my reputation. Not in my comfort. Not in my platform. Not in my marriage or my kids or my home or my health. In You. Because anything else I get established in will eventually try to replace You. That is just how it works. Whatever holds me up will start to feel like it is the thing I need most. And the moment I forget who is actually holding me up, I am one step away from drifting. I do not want to be a Rehoboam. I do not want to follow one either. I want to stay close to God in the seasons of plenty the same way I clung to Him in the seasons of need. Where in your life have you gotten so comfortable that you have started drifting from the One who got you there?

entries.title: He Did Not Even Pray
entries.description: Asa got sick and went straight to his doctors. He did not even pray. The same king who once cried out to God against an army of a million.
entries.body: "In the thirty-ninth year of his reign, Asa developed a serious foot disease. Yet even with the severity of his disease, he did not seek the Lord's help but turned only to his physicians." 2 Chronicles 16:12 (NLT) I think I highlighted this one as a reminder. We are blessed to have doctors. We are blessed to have medicine and surgery and specialists who can diagnose things our ancestors would have just died from. I am thankful for physicians. Truly. But this verse is not saying doctors are wrong. It is saying Asa turned only to his physicians. Only. He did not turn to the Lord at all. And what stood out to me is that a lot of people, when something serious happens, that is when they finally seek God. A scary diagnosis. A bad accident. A test that comes back wrong. Hard things have a way of softening people and turning their eyes upward. But Asa did not even do that. He had a serious disease. The kind of thing that would normally drive a person to their knees. And he just went to the doctors. He did not pray. He did not seek God. He did not even cry out. That is part of what makes this story so sad. Because this is the same Asa who, earlier in his reign, cried out to God when an enemy army of a million men came against him. He prayed Lord, no one but you can help the powerless against the mighty. And God showed up. Same king. Different posture. When he was younger, he ran to God first. When he was older, he ran to God last. Or in this case, not at all. That progression is sobering. It is so easy to slowly stop including God in the things that matter. To trust the doctor instead of asking the doctor and the Lord. To trust the expert instead of seeking the One who made the expert. To go straight to the solution and skip past the One who can actually heal. I do not want to be that person. I want to be someone who prays and goes to the doctor. Someone who asks God for wisdom, and reads the book. Someone who seeks Him first and then gets the advice. Not instead of help. Alongside it. Above it. Because the help is good. But the Lord is the one who decides how the help actually plays out. When something hard hits, where do you go first?

entries.title: Solomon Decided
entries.description: Scripture says Solomon decided to build the temple. But we just finished 1 Chronicles. We know the rest of the story.
entries.body: "Solomon decided to build a Temple to honor the name of the Lord, and also a royal palace for himself." 2 Chronicles 2:1 (NLT) If you read my last blog, you will get why this verse caught me. David did basically everything but the building itself. He had the plans. He organized the materials. He set aside the gold and silver. He passed on the instructions to Solomon and said the Lord gave me every detail of this in writing. David did the work behind the work. Then I turn the page into 2 Chronicles, just a few chapters later, and the first verse says this. Solomon decided to build a Temple to honor the name of the Lord, and also a royal palace for himself. Solomon decided. That phrasing is what got me. It is almost like whoever wrote 2 Chronicles is picking up the story without the full backstory. Like they are just recording what they knew. Solomon decided to start building. That was the moment from their angle. But we, the readers, just got done with 1 Chronicles. We know it was not really Solomon's decision in the way it sounds. We know David had been preparing for this for years. We know God told David the plans Himself. We know Solomon was inheriting all of it. And yet right here, the verse just credits Solomon with the decision. It is a good reminder that the Bible is real history written by real people. Not every chapter has the full picture. Some chapters are someone telling what they saw. Some chapters are someone giving the highlights. Some chapters are someone filling in details that were missing. That is part of what makes Scripture so rich. You have to read it together, not in isolated pieces. One book gives you part of the story. Another book gives you the rest. If you only had 2 Chronicles, you might think Solomon woke up one day and decided to build a temple all on his own. But because we have 1 Chronicles, we know better. We know the years of preparation. We know the father who prayed and planned and passed it on. We know it was God's idea long before it was anyone's decision. It also makes me think about how God works in ways that span generations. The temple was on God's heart long before Solomon was born. David carried it. Solomon built it. And somewhere in heaven, God knew the full thread from beginning to end. That is the bigger story. Not who got the credit. Not who got the headline. Just God moving across generations to do what He set out to do. And He is still doing that. He is still working in ways that started before us and will continue after us. He is still weaving plans through families and prayers and quiet faithfulness. He is still the one whose idea it all was in the first place. Have you ever realized that something good in your life was actually started by someone before you, who never got to see how it played out?

entries.title: 2 Chronicles 20:15
entries.description: The battle is not yours, but God
entries.body: "He said, 'Listen, all you people of Judah and Jerusalem! Listen, King Jehoshaphat! This is what the Lord says: Do not be afraid! Don't be discouraged by this mighty army, for the battle is not yours, but God's.'" 2 Chronicles 20:15 (NLT) We say it all the time. The battle belongs to the Lord. And usually when we say it, we are thinking of David and Goliath. The little guy with a sling, running toward a giant, declaring that the battle was the Lord's. And then he picked up a stone and fought. So we read that and we think, okay, God leads us, but we still have to fight the battle in front of us. And then this verse shows up. Same phrase. The battle is not yours, but God's. But this time, the next line is different. You will not even need to fight. That is the part I keep going back to. Sometimes God says the battle is mine and I am going to use you to fight it. And sometimes God says the battle is mine and you do not even need to lift a finger. Both are true. Both are biblical. But we tend to default to the first one. We think we always have to do something. Strategize. Push. Hustle. Plan. Fight. And there are absolutely seasons for that. David had his sling. We have our slings too. But there are also seasons where God says sit down. Watch. I have got this one. And those might be the hardest ones to obey, honestly. Because doing nothing while you are surrounded by a mighty army feels insane. But that is exactly what Judah was told to do. Just show up, take your positions, stand still, and watch the Lord rescue you. There is one more piece of this story that I love. Right before this word came from the Lord, all the people of Judah were standing before God praying. The verse says the men of Judah stood before the Lord. But it does not stop there. It goes on to say they were standing there with their little ones, their wives, and their children. The whole family was there. They got to witness the prayer. They got to hear the word from the Lord. They got to be part of the miracle. The kids were not off in another room being entertained. They were right there in the middle of it. I want that for my family too. I want my little ones and my kids and my people to be part of the instructions. Part of the prayers. Part of the moments when God speaks. Part of the miracles when He shows up. Not just told about it later. Right there in it. Because faith caught in the room is different than faith taught from a distance. Where in your life is God saying you do not even need to fight, just stand still and watch? And who in your family is in the room with you while He is speaking?

entries.title: 2 Chronicles 22:12
entries.description: A baby hidden in the temple for six years while a wicked queen thought she had won. God
entries.body: "Joash remained hidden in the Temple of God for six years while Athaliah ruled the land." 2 Chronicles 22:12 (NLT) This is one of those stories that almost reads like a movie. Here is what is happening. The king dies. And his mother, Athaliah, decides she wants the throne. So she starts killing the rest of the royal family. Including her own grandchildren. Let that sit for a second. A grandmother killing her grandchildren so she can rule. But one of her grandchildren got away. The king's sister, Jehoshabeath, grabbed her infant nephew Joash before Athaliah could get to him. She hid him, along with his nurse, and then took him to the temple where her husband was the priest. And that is where he stayed. For six years. A baby. Then a toddler. Then a small boy. Hidden in the temple of God while his grandmother sat on a throne that was not hers, murdering anyone who got in her way. How do you even hide an infant for six years? Babies cry. Toddlers run. Kids ask questions. And somehow, with the help of God, this child stayed hidden in plain sight in one of the most sacred places in the kingdom. That is the part I cannot get over. God had a plan for this little boy. A throne that was rightfully his. A future the rest of his family was murdered before they could see. And while a wicked queen sat on the throne thinking she had wiped out the line of David, God had quietly preserved it. One baby. Hidden in His house. Protected for His purpose. I love that the temple was the place where Joash was kept safe. The very place dedicated to God became the very place that protected the next king. The line of David ran straight through the house of God. The future of an entire kingdom was kept alive in the building where God's people came to worship. That feels like a picture of something bigger. God's purposes do not get cancelled by the schemes of people in power. They get hidden. Quietly. Carefully. Sometimes for years. And then He brings them back out when the time is right. I think about how often I assume something has been ruined because of what someone else did. Or because of the season I am in. Or because of how long it has been. And the truth is, sometimes what feels like silence is actually God hiding something safe until the right moment. Athaliah ruled for six years thinking she had won. She had not. There was a boy in the temple. And he was the rightful king. God's plans are not as fragile as we think they are. And He is not running out of time. Even when everything around us looks like the wrong people are winning, He is preserving what matters in places we cannot see. Where in your life have you assumed something was lost, when God might be quietly protecting it for the right moment?

entries.title: The Gospel Hiding in the Law
entries.description: An old law about not punishing children for their parents
entries.body: "However, he did not kill the children of the assassins, for he obeyed the command of the Lord as written by Moses in the Book of the Law: 'Parents must not be put to death for the sins of their children, nor children for the sins of their parents. Those deserving to die must be put to death for their own crimes.'" 2 Chronicles 25:4 (NLT) The context here is a little dark. Amaziah is now king, and the men who assassinated his father have been brought to justice. He has them executed. But he stops there. He does not touch their children. He could have. In that culture, it would have been completely normal to wipe out the families of your enemies. To make sure no son of an assassin grew up wanting revenge. To protect the throne by erasing the whole line. He does not do it. Because the law said no. Parents must not be put to death for the sins of their children. Nor children for the sins of their parents. Those deserving to die must be put to death for their own crimes. That law was given through Moses hundreds of years before this moment. And it was protecting the next generation in a way that the world around them was not protecting anyone. I think this is what stood out to me when I highlighted it. Because that principle, even buried in the law of Moses, was pointing to something much bigger. It was pointing to Jesus. Every person stands before God on their own. You do not get punished for what your parents did. You do not get saved by what your grandparents believed. You do not inherit someone else's righteousness. You do not inherit someone else's guilt. Each person answers for their own life. That is the law. But then look what God does through Jesus. The very God who said no one can die for another person's crime is the same God who sent His Son to do exactly that. Not because the law was broken. But because the law had a deeper truth running underneath it. The law said no human can take another human's punishment. But Jesus was not just a human. He was the spotless Lamb of God. He was the only one who could take on the punishment of another, because He had no punishment of His own to deal with. He did not deserve to die. So He could die for those who did. That is the gospel hiding inside this little verse about Amaziah. The same God who told Israel you cannot pay for someone else's sin later said but I can. And I will. That is what the law was always leading to. The law showed us how impossible it was to save ourselves. It set the standard. It drew the line. It made the boundaries clear. And then Jesus came and met the standard, walked the line, and stepped across the boundary on our behalf. I love finding little glimpses of Jesus in places I would not expect. Tucked into a chapter about a king and his enemies and a quote from an old law. The whole Bible is like that. It is one big story pointing in one direction. His name is Jesus. What is a place in the Old Testament where you have seen Jesus hiding in plain sight?

entries.title: What Rises in Pride
entries.description: Uzziah started well. Then he got powerful, got proud, and forgot the rules applied to him. The pattern is not new. It is not just for famous people either.
entries.body: "But when he had become powerful, he also became proud, which led to his downfall. He sinned against the Lord his God by entering the sanctuary of the Lord's Temple and personally burning incense on the incense altar." 2 Chronicles 26:16 (NLT) What we see playing out in our culture today is not new. That is the first thing I thought reading this. This is King Uzziah. He started off as a good king. He sought God. He listened to wise counsel. God's hand was on him in a powerful way. He won battles. He built things. He grew strong. The Bible literally says his fame spread far and wide because God helped him in marvelous ways. But then. When he had become powerful, he also became proud, which led to his downfall. It is the same story we see over and over. God puts His hand on someone's ministry. They start gaining a following. People listen to them. People love them. The platform grows. The influence grows. And somewhere along the way, they forget where the power came from in the first place. They start to think the rules do not apply to them anymore. That is what happened with Uzziah. He walked into the temple to burn incense himself. Which sounds harmless. Right? He was the king. He loved God. He was worshipping. Why would burning incense be a bad thing? Because only the priests were allowed to do it. God had been very clear about that. There was a specific role for the king and a specific role for the priest. Uzziah knew it. Everyone knew it. But he had gotten powerful enough that he thought he could redraw the line. The priests confronted him. Eighty of them. Brave men of God who walked right up to the king and said this is not for you to do. Leave the sanctuary. And here is the part that breaks me. He did not humble himself. He got angry. He puffed up. He stood there in the middle of the temple, holding the incense, and basically said I am the king. I can do this if I want to. And in that exact moment, leprosy broke out on his forehead. His life was destroyed in front of everyone. He was rushed out of the temple. He lived in isolation the rest of his life. His son had to take over the kingdom for him. The reign that had been so blessed ended in shame. I want to be careful with this story, because it is easy to read it and just point fingers at famous pastors and influencers who have fallen. And there have been a lot. The pattern is the same. God's hand. A following. Pride. A line crossed. A public collapse. We do not have leprosy now. We have social media. We have headlines. We have receipts and screenshots and stories that go everywhere within hours. The exposure looks different. But the principle is the same. What rises in pride will fall in public. And the warning is not just for the famous person. It is for me too. Because I am not above this pattern. None of us are. The moment I start thinking I have earned what God gave me, I am one step from where Uzziah was. The moment I start thinking the rules apply to everyone except me, I am right there. The moment I get corrected and respond with anger instead of humility, I am holding the incense. God resists the proud. Not in a small way. Not in a quiet way. He actively resists. I want to be the kind of person who, when corrected, drops the incense and walks out. Not the kind who argues my way into a downfall. When was the last time you were corrected, and how did you actually respond?

entries.title: Careful
entries.description: Jotham took the good of his father
entries.body: "King Jotham became powerful because he was careful to live in obedience to the Lord his God." 2 Chronicles 27:6 (NLT) This is the son of the king I wrote about in the last blog. Uzziah. The one who started off so well and ended in pride and disgrace. The one who walked into the temple thinking he was above the rules and walked out with leprosy. Now we meet his son Jotham. And the Bible says something so important about him. It says he did what was right in the sight of the Lord, just as his father had done. However, he did not enter the temple of the Lord. He did what his father did. Except for the sin. He took the good. And he left the bad. That is one of the most hopeful sentences in this whole section of Scripture. Because we do not have to repeat the failures of the generations before us. That is not always easy to believe. There is a lot of teaching out there about generational patterns and family cycles and how the same struggles repeat themselves over and over in a bloodline. And some of that is true. We do pick things up from the people who raised us. We do inherit habits and tendencies and even wounds. But the story of Jotham is the story of a son who decided that what tripped his father up was not going to trip him up. He honored the parts of his father's life worth honoring. The pursuit of God. The leadership. The accomplishments. The good legacy was kept. But when it came to the place where his father fell, Jotham drew a line. There is one word in this verse that I do not want to skip past. Careful. King Jotham became powerful because he was careful to live in obedience to the Lord his God. Not accidentally obedient. Not naturally obedient. Careful. That word means it was intentional. Watchful. Guarded. He paid attention to his life. He paid attention to his steps. He paid attention to the place his father went wrong, and he made sure he did not drift there himself. That is not how most of us live. We mostly just go. We mostly just react. We mostly just do the next thing in front of us and hope it adds up to a good life. We are not careful. We are not watchful. We are not paying close attention to the patterns in our family or the line we promised God we were not going to cross. Jotham was different. He watched. He guarded. He chose. And the Bible directly ties his power to that carefulness. He became powerful because he was careful to obey. His blessing came from his intentionality. We do not break cycles by hoping things turn out differently. We break them by being careful. By noticing where the pull is strongest. By naming the patterns. By saying out loud, that was my dad's struggle. It will not be mine. Not because I am stronger. Because I am paying attention. If your parents struggled with anger, be careful. If they drank, be careful. If they avoided God, be careful. If they walked away from the church, be careful. If they were unfaithful, be careful. If they ran, be careful. You are not stuck. But you do have to be aware. The patterns can break. The cycles can stop. But it takes carefulness. The kind Jotham had. The kind that does not drift but actually chooses, day after day, to live the opposite of the wrong example. What is one place in your life where you need to be more careful than you have been?

entries.title: 2 Chronicles 28:23
entries.description: King Ahaz worshipped the gods of the army that defeated him, and it ruined him. A reflection on why borrowed gods never bless.
entries.body: "He offered sacrifices to the gods of Damascus who had defeated him, for he said, 'Since these gods helped the kings of Aram, they will help me, too, if I sacrifice to them.' But instead, they led to his ruin and the ruin of all Israel." 2 Chronicles 28:23 (NLT) This story is so backwards it almost does not make sense. King Ahaz of Judah is in trouble. The Arameans have just defeated him. His army got crushed. His people are suffering. He is losing on every side. So what does he do? He decides to start worshipping the gods of the people who just beat him. Read that again. He looked at the army that just destroyed him and thought well, their gods must be working. If I worship those gods too, maybe they will help me the way they helped them. So he sacrificed to the gods of his enemies. The ones who had nothing to do with the God of Israel. The ones who actually had nothing to do with the victory at all. And he tried to use them to fix his life. The verse says they led to his ruin and the ruin of all Israel. I think about how often we do this exact thing. We look around at people who seem successful. People whose lives look like they are working. People who have the money, the marriage, the platform, the followers, the house, the body, the calm and put-together image. And we copy them. Even if they do not love God. Even if their whole foundation is built on something other than Him. We figure if it works for them, it will work for us. So we adopt their habits. Their priorities. Their ways of thinking. Their version of success. We try to bring their gods into our house, thinking it might give us what they have. And it ruins us. Just like it ruined Ahaz. Because what we cannot see is that someone else's so-called success is not the whole story. We are seeing the highlight reel. We are not seeing the emptiness. We are not seeing the broken relationships. We are not seeing the anxiety, the addiction, the spiritual deadness, the slow drift away from anything real. We see the win. And we want it. So we sacrifice to their gods. We try the thing that worked for them, hoping it will work for us, even when we know deep down it is not from God. But borrowed gods do not bless. They consume. They led to ruin then. And they lead to ruin now. The thing that struck me about Ahaz is that he had access to the real God. He was a king of Judah. His own father had walked with God. He had the temple. He had the priests. He had the scrolls. He had every resource available to seek the Lord. But he chose foreign gods instead. I do not want to be that. I do not want to chase the formulas of people who look successful on the outside while ignoring the God I already have access to. I do not want to copy somebody else's life because it looks like it is working. I do not want to drift into worship of things God never told me to worship just because the world keeps telling me they are the answer. The God who has been with me from the beginning is the God who knows the way through. I do not need to borrow somebody else's. Where in your life have you been tempted to copy someone whose foundation is not God, hoping it will work for you too?

entries.title: I Have No Idea Why I Highlighted This
entries.description: Sometimes you come back to a verse you highlighted and have no memory of why. That is part of what makes the Bible alive.
entries.body: "Solomon ruled over all the kings from the Euphrates River in the north to the land of the Philistines and the border of Egypt in the south." 2 Chronicles 9:26 (NLT) I have to be honest. I do not know why I highlighted this one. I actually thought about just skipping blogging about it. I was reading the Bible in a month, just moving through it, marking what stood out in the moment. I did not jot notes. I did not stop and journal about it. I just highlighted and kept going. So now I am looking at it a few months later trying to figure out what caught me. And I have no idea. But here is the thing. This happens to me all the time when I open my Bible. I will be reading and come across a verse that I highlighted years ago. Or a little note I scribbled in the margin. And I have no memory of why. I do not remember what season I was in or what I was wrestling with or what God was saying to me when I marked it. But I have come to love that about reading Scripture. Because it means the Bible is alive in a way other books just are not. You can read a verse five years ago and something in it grabs you. It speaks to exactly where you are. You highlight it because you cannot let it go. And then five years later you read the same verse and something completely different stands out. A different word. A different angle. A different lesson. The verse did not change. You did. God meets you in the Word right where you are. The same verse can comfort you in one season and challenge you in another. It can be a promise one year and a warning the next. It can hold a memory of where you were when you first read it, and at the same time be brand new. That is what makes the Bible so different from anything else. So for this verse, I will probably never know why I highlighted it. Maybe I just thought it was cool that Solomon's reach was that far. Maybe I was thinking about how much God blessed him. Maybe I was tired and my highlighter slipped. lol I do not know. But what stands out to me now, reading it again, is that all of this happened because David asked God for guidance. Because Solomon asked God for wisdom. Because generations of obedience added up to a kingdom that stretched from the Euphrates to Egypt. That is what stuck out today. It might be something completely different the next time I read it. And that is okay. That is part of why the Bible is so cool. You never read the same verse twice, even when the words have not changed. Have you ever come back to a verse you highlighted in the past and had no idea why? What do you think God is showing you now in it?

entries.title: 2 Kings 2:17
entries.description: Right after the mountaintop, Elisha gets shamed into something he knew was wrong. A reflection on how being chosen by God does not make you immune to people-pleasing.
entries.body: "But they kept urging him until they shamed him into agreeing, and he finally said, 'All right, send them.' So fifty men searched for three days but did not find Elijah." 2 Kings 2:17 (NLT) This whole moment is wild. Elijah is taken up in a whirlwind. Flaming horses, a chariot of fire, the whole thing. Elisha sees it happen. He picks up Elijah's cloak, walks down to the Jordan, hits the water with it, and asks where the God of Elijah is. And the river parts. So now Elisha has the cloak. He has just seen something almost no one in history has seen. He has the visible confirmation that God's hand is on him. And then this happens.
